sections.title: How does GeoNet monitor Ruapehu?
sections.body: GeoNet has several monitoring stations in the Ngāti Rangi rohe. These stations are used to monitor volcanic activity and work together with other stations all around Aotearoa New Zealand to monitor earthquakes, volcanoes, landslides and tsunami. At Ruapehu (and other active volcanoes), GeoNet also periodically collect gas and water measurements. These data help inform communities and agencies about volcano behaviour and potential impacts. All data are freely and openly available to everyone and can be viewed and downloaded through the GeoNet website and other GeoNet tools.

sections.title: Mangateitei station
sections.body: Just north of Ohakune, the Mangateitei station is located on the southern side of Mount Ruapehu. Different types of instruments are installed at the station. A seismometer to measure earthquakes, tremors and seismic activity, a GNSS (or GPS) to measure ground deformation and a web camera to have a view on the volcano. All these data are continuously recorded and transmitted in real-time to GeoNet. As soon as GeoNet receive them, data are made freely available to the public through the GeoNet website and other GeoNet tools.

sections.title: Volcano monitoring cameras
sections.body: GeoNet's volcano camera images are an important part of the monitoring programme as changes at a volcano can be observed and compared over time. GeoNet cameras produce an image every 10 minutes. The latest images can be viewed on the Volcano Cameras page on the GeoNet website.

sections.title: Mangateitei Web Camera
sections.body: If we fly back to Mangateitei station, the visual camera installed provides images of Mount Ruapehu from the South. Mangateitei webcam latest images can be viewed on the Ruapehu South camera page. The full archive of high resolution images since 2011, when the camera was first installed, can be downloaded on the GeoNet Data portal. The station code for this camera is MTSR.
